To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the primary systemic therapy of patients with early breast cancer should be based on: 1) accurate and reliable determination of the expression of the oestrogen receptor (ER), HER2 and other markers of prognosis and/or response, 2) the risk of relapse of the individual patient as defined by clinical and pathological factors and the results of these tests, and 3) the potential benefit of the proposed treatment in the light of these data and other relevant clinical information.

(1) endocrine therapy should be given to all ER positive patients with early breast cancer; (2) HER2 positive patients with early stage breast cancer should receive anti HER2 therapy; and (3) adjuvant cytotoxic chemotherapy should be given to high risk patients with early stage disease.

(i) ER+ tumours should be treated with endocrine therapy unless the tumour is very low risk (e.g. node negative, low grade, low Ki67, low recurrence score) (ii) ER- tumours should be considered for chemotherapy unless they are very low risk (iii) HER2+ tumours should receive anti HER2 therapy unless the tumours are very low risk.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the molecular determinants of the response to endocrine therapy.
the identification of new therapeutic targets, and the development of new therapies, which are effective and have minimal side effects.
the development of new therapies for cancer and with the improvement of the quality of life for patients suffering from cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the threshold for adjuvant therapy of early breast cancer is a positive ER level, overexpression or amplification by standard criteria of HER2 and a high risk of recurrence as defined by clinical and pathological factors, including the results of multigene array assays.
adjuvant therapy should be targeted according to predictive biomarker status and the level of risk of relapse, with a caveat that the predictive markers should be reliably and accurately determined.

the primary treatment of breast cancer is best determined by a multidisciplinary team, using a risk assessment based on the individual tumour characteristics and patient factors, to determine the most appropriate treatment for each patient, including surgery, radiotherapy, endocrine therapy, anti-HER2 therapy, and chemotherapy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the threshold for indication of adjuvant systemic therapy depends on the risk of relapse and the risk of death, which in turn depends on the biology of the tumour, the stage of the disease and other patient factors.
the St Gallen group has made a significant contribution to the development of the current understanding and management of early breast cancer.
the primary treatment of breast cancer has become more complex but is now better defined.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the primary treatment of breast cancer is now based on the molecular characteristics of the tumour.
the St Gallen panel has not abandoned the concept of risk assessment, but rather has refined it to include the role of predictive markers.
the threshold for adjuvant systemic therapy should be set at the level of the individual patient, not the population.
